name: Double Definiteness
explanation: When an adjective comes before a definite noun, Danish adds a separate article — "den" (common gender), "det" (neuter), or "de" (plural) — in front of the adjective. The noun itself then stays in its plain, unsuffixed form; it does not also take "-en/-et/-ene". This combination of the free-standing article plus the unsuffixed noun is called double definiteness.

examples.danish: Det store hus ligger på hjørnet.
examples.english: The big house is on the corner.

examples.danish: Jeg kan godt lide den røde dør.
examples.english: I really like the red door.

name: Adjective Inflection in Definite Form
explanation: In a definite noun phrase, the adjective always takes the ending "-e", no matter the noun's gender or number. This differs from indefinite phrases, where the adjective's ending changes: "et stort hus" (neuter, "-t") becomes "det store hus" (definite, "-e"); "en stor stol" (common gender, no ending) becomes "den store stol" (definite, "-e").

examples.danish: Vi har lige malet det gamle skab.
examples.english: We just painted the old cabinet.

examples.danish: De nye møbler passer godt i stuen.
examples.english: The new furniture fits well in the living room.

name: Predicative vs. Attributive Adjectives
explanation: An attributive adjective sits directly before the noun and triggers double definiteness and the "-e" ending in definite phrases (den store lejlighed). A predicative adjective comes after a linking verb like "være" and instead follows the regular indefinite agreement pattern, even when the subject is definite: "Lejligheden er stor" (not "store").

examples.danish: Den lyse stue er mit yndlingssted i huset.
examples.english: The bright living room is my favorite spot in the house.

examples.danish: Stuen er lys og hyggelig om aftenen.
examples.english: The living room is bright and cozy in the evening.
